real_bugs_found_and_fixed_this_milestone.bug: reconcile_expired's RECOVERABLE_EXPIRED_STATES mapped CANCEL_REQUESTED -> CANCEL_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN, a mapping written for a worker that transition_worker'd into CANCEL_REQUESTED under its own live lease and died before calling the provider. That scenario has zero production callers; the only real writer of CANCEL_REQUESTED is D1's unfenced request_cancel, whose lease is stale by construction. Left in place, the first scan after any cancel request would have folded the attempt to CANCEL_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN (then NEEDS_OPERATOR for a NONE-idempotency provider) without ever attempting the provider call.

real_bugs_found_and_fixed_this_milestone.bug: realize_pending_cancels' fence acquisition used the same liveness-gated acquire_lease as reconcile_expired, but request_cancel never touches the lease -- a realistic cancel request (users cancel within minutes of submitting) could land while the submission-phase lease's 300s TTL had not yet elapsed, arbitrarily delaying a legitimate cancel for no correctness reason.

real_bugs_found_and_fixed_this_milestone.bug: The legacy orphan-recovery handler (ADR 0007, lib/generation_worker.py's _handle_orphan_tasks_on_start) is the system that actually makes every real restart-recovery decision today; it operates entirely on the legacy tasks table and never touches execution_attempts. Without a bridge, execution_attempts would go permanently stale the moment a real crash happened: the attempt would sit ACCEPTED forever while the legacy system correctly resolved the task's real fate through its own, unrelated mechanism.
real_bugs_found_and_fixed_this_milestone.fix: bfa4770d -- GenerationQueue.mark_task_succeeded/failed/cancelled (the single choke point every finalization path -- normal executor, every orphan-handler branch, and its background resume dispatcher -- funnels through) now mirror the already-decided outcome into execution_attempts, without changing any of that decision logic. A direct ACCEPTED/RUNNING -> CANCELLED fact has no legal edge in the attempt state machine (cancellation requires a recorded intent first); the mirror synthesizes one via request_cancel before applying the CANCELLED observation.
real_bugs_found_and_fixed_this_milestone.reachability_at_discovery: structural gap present since M7-A; found while researching whether the ACCEPTED/RUNNING lease-heartbeat design (originally planned) was actually necessary. real_bugs_found_and_fixed_this_milestone.bug: Test-infrastructure flake in this milestone's own new tests: test_generation_queue_execution_attempts_mirror.py, test_realize_pending_cancels.py, test_execution_recovery_scan.py, and test_execution_recovery_scheduler.py each anchored a lease's expires_at to a module-level REAL_NOW = datetime.now(UTC) evaluated once at collection time, plus a fixed timedelta(minutes=5). Under the full postgres-compat selection (~1000 tests, 4 xdist workers, real wall-clock collection-to-execution gap under system load), that margin was exceeded for these modules, so acquire_lease's own real 'not yet expired' check in transition_worker legitimately (and correctly) raised ExecutionAttemptFencingError -- 11 spurious failures, first surfaced only under the full CI-exact selection, never in isolated or SQLite runs.
real_bugs_found_and_fixed_this_milestone.fix: Each expires_at=REAL_NOW + timedelta(minutes=5) call site changed to expires_at=datetime.now(UTC) + timedelta(minutes=5), computed fresh at actual call time instead of at module import time. created_at/observed_at uses of REAL_NOW (static test data, never compared against live now()) were left unchanged.
real_bugs_found_and_fixed_this_milestone.reachability_at_discovery: test-only; the fencing logic itself behaved correctly (a truly expired lease must be rejected). Note: tests/integration/lib/db/repositories/test_execution_attempt_repository.py (a pre-existing, already-accepted M7-A/M7-B file) has the identical REAL_NOW-anchored-lease pattern at ~20 call sites and carries the same latent risk; it did not fail this run and was left untouched as out of this file's scope.

architecture_decision_this_milestone.question: Should H5 recovery for ACCEPTED/RUNNING attempts be built as (a) a full happy-path migration onto host-hardening polling, or (b) a narrow restart-scanner extension that leaves the live, non-crashed happy path untouched?
architecture_decision_this_milestone.answer: (b), and this was not a new decision -- the original 2026-09-12 M7 research (docs/research/2026-09-12-r2-m7-host-production-hardening-research.md sections 2.4 and 4.1) had already settled on a narrow restart scanner ('nó không biến mọi running task thành queued'). Re-read and cited before building anything, per the repository's research-first rule.
architecture_decision_this_milestone.resolution: The bookkeeping mirror (bfa4770d) turned out to close the correctness gap for ACCEPTED/RUNNING entirely on its own, since execution_attempts becomes truthful within a bounded number of restarts via the same choke point every completion path already shares. No lease-heartbeat, no ACCEPTED/RUNNING poller, and no changes to any of the 7 video backends were needed.

real_sigkill_evidence.method: A real, separate OS process (subprocess.Popen) durably commits an attempt to SUBMITTING or CANCEL_REQUESTED against a real file-backed SQLite database, signals readiness via a sentinel file, then blocks forever. The test process sends a real os.kill(pid, SIGKILL), reaps the process, confirms a non-zero/hard-kill exit code, then runs the recovery scan from itself -- a genuinely different, still-alive process -- against the same database file.
real_sigkill_evidence.why_sqlite_not_postgres: A real subprocess needs its own DB connection regardless of dialect, so this does not need PostgreSQL to prove cross-process survival; :memory: SQLite cannot be shared across processes, so file_session_factory (real file-backed SQLite, sqlite_only marker) is used instead. Concurrency-under-load claims elsewhere in M7-C are separately proven against real PostgreSQL (see gate_results.pytest_postgres_compat).
cases_proven: SIGKILL mid-SUBMITTING: the killed process's lease genuinely expires in real wall-clock time; reconcile_expired (run from the live test process) reclaims it and resolves it to NEEDS_OPERATOR, matching Kling's real NONE-idempotency capability profile (no safe reconciliation).

SIGKILL immediately after a cancel intent is recorded: realize_pending_cancels (run from the live test process) attempts the cancel against Kling's real capability profile (supports_cancel: false), and the intent survives the crash exactly as CANCEL_REQUESTED -- never lost, never falsely resolved to CANCELLED or FAILED.

live_process_wiring.wired_in: server/app.py's lifespan, started/stopped alongside (but independent of) GenerationWorker
live_process_wiring.independence_from_generation_worker: The scheduler only ever touches execution_attempts; GenerationWorker's orphan handler only ever touches the legacy tasks table (bridged one-way by the bookkeeping mirror above). There is no shared mutable state between them to coordinate.
live_process_wiring.adapter_resolver_note: build_adapter_resolver(default_to_unsupported=True) is used for this scheduler. Every currently registered capability profile (checked against the real registry, r2/provider_capabilities/registry.json, all 11 entries) declares idempotency_mode=NONE and supports_cancel=false, so reconcile()'s adapter-dependent qualified-lookup path never reaches an adapter at all today, and a real cancel() would fail exactly like the fallback already does. This is behaviorally identical to a fully wired adapter registry for everything currently registered, not a shortcut -- documented in docs/research/2026-09-20-r2-m7c-poll-download-cancel-design.md section 5. The default-raise-loud behavior (NoAdapterRegisteredError) is preserved unchanged for submit, which must still fail loud on a genuine misconfiguration.

coverage_limitations: No independent (Codex or otherwise) review was run against this exact HEAD; status is a human/self override per status_note above.

PostgreSQL testing used fresh, empty, single-node local Docker containers (postgres:16-alpine); it does not exercise production-scale connection pooling, replica failover, or the CI runner's exact resource profile. Process note for future local reproduction: tests/conftest.py's async_session fixture (used by legacy repo tests, distinct from the per-test-schema session_factory fixture most of this suite uses) deliberately does not run migrations when DATABASE_URL is externally provided -- it trusts the CI job's own prior `alembic upgrade head` step. A local run against a brand-new container must run that migration manually first, or every async_session-based test fails with UndefinedTableError (this cost real time to diagnose in this session; see real_bugs_found_and_fixed_this_milestone for the two other, genuine test-authoring bugs found alongside it).

The real SIGKILL tests prove cross-process survival on file-backed SQLite; they do not additionally prove it on PostgreSQL, since the mechanism under test (a real process death and a fenced CAS reclaim) is dialect-independent and PostgreSQL-specific concurrency claims are separately proven elsewhere in this file's pytest_postgres_compat results.

No real backend currently supports cancel, so realize_pending_cancels' successful-cancellation and ambiguous-failure paths are proven only against fakes, never against a real provider's real HTTP API.

ACCEPTED/RUNNING attempts are made truthful only when the underlying task actually reaches a terminal legacy outcome (success/fail/cancel) through the existing orphan-recovery or normal-completion path; there is no independent, faster-than-natural-completion detection of a hung/stuck ACCEPTED/RUNNING attempt in this milestone.
Provider qualification (ADR-0089 P0 item 3's second half) and M7-D's backup/restore drill are explicitly out of scope for this file; see deferred_work above.
Frontend (pnpm check) and website checks were not run in this session; M7-C touched zero files under frontend/ or website/ (confirmed via git diff --stat against the M7-B head).
